title: Superficial muscles of the posterior leg (posterior)

rows: Lateral surface of the lateral condyle of the femur.
Posterior surface of the calcaneus through the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon.
Plantarflexes the foot at the ankle, most strongly when the knee is straight, and helps flex the leg at the knee.
Popliteal surface of the femur, just above the medial condyle.
Posterior surface of the calcaneus through the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon.
Plantarflexes the foot at the ankle, most strongly when the knee is straight, and helps flex the leg at the knee.
Back of the head and upper quarter of the fibula, the soleal line and medial border of the tibia, and a tendinous arch between the two bones.
Posterior surface of the calcaneus through the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon.
Plantarflexes the foot at the ankle whatever the position of the knee. Steadies the leg on the foot in standing.
Lower end of the lateral supracondylar line of the femur.
Posterior surface of the calcaneus, by a long thin tendon that usually runs along the medial side of the calcaneal tendon and may blend with it.
Weakly helps gastrocnemius plantarflex the foot and flex the leg at the knee. The muscle is absent in about one limb in ten.
Common tendon of gastrocnemius and soleus, inserting on the posterior surface of the calcaneus.
Carries the pull of the calf muscles to the heel for plantarflexion. It is the thickest and strongest tendon of the body.
hy: Tapping it tests the ankle jerk reflex (S1, S2).

A rupture gives sudden pain in the calf, often with a snap, and weak plantarflexion. Squeezing the calf then fails to plantarflex the foot (Thompson test). Fluoroquinolone antibiotics raise the risk of rupture.
